title: Partition Shapes into Equal Parts
goal: I can make and recognize equal-area parts of one whole.
catchAll: Equal parts must cover the same amount of the whole. Counting pieces alone is not enough.

teacher.def: The denominator of a fraction tells how many equal parts are in the whole. It is the bottom part of the fraction
A unit fraction is ONE part of a whole. It always has a numerator of one.
The numerator of a fraction tells how many equal parts are being described. It is the top part of the fraction.
A fraction is a number used when a whole is split into equal parts.

glossary.whole: the one shape, unit length, complete piece or entire set named in the question
glossary.partition: divide a whole into equal parts
glossary.interval: the distance between neighboring marks on a number line

screens.title: Name the whole
text: A whole can be divided in different ways.

screens.title: Connect the parts
text: Equal parts have equal area, even when their shapes look different.
Equal parts must cover the same amount of the whole. Counting pieces alone is not enough.

screens.title: Check the reasoning
text: More equal parts of the same whole make each part smaller.

item.prompt: How can you tell whether the parts of a shape are equal? Write a complete sentence.
item.example: I can check that every part covers the same amount of the whole, rather than just counting how many pieces I see.
hints: Describe what the whole is and how its parts are counted.
show: Compare your reasoning with a grown-up or the model response.
I can check that every part covers the same amount of the whole, rather than just counting how many pieces I see.

steps.say: Start with one rectangular strip. Its entire area is one whole.
Fold the strip into two matching halves, then fold both halves in half again.
Open the strip. The four full-height sections have equal widths, so their areas are equal.
Check that the four sections cover the strip once, without gaps or overlap.
Use one new rectangular strip as the whole.
Mark its length into six equal distances. Draw a dividing line straight across at each inside mark.
Each section has the same width and height. There are six equal areas, called sixths.
Joining each pair of neighboring sections would make three larger equal areas.
Start with one round disk as the whole.
Fold it in half, then in half again, then in half once more.
Unfold the disk. Eight equal sectors meet at the center.
All eight parts cover the same area; the number of pieces alone would not prove this if the folds were unequal.

Changing the whole halfway through a question.
